item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
I think Hiemal may refer to "hibernation" here, given they both come from the same latin word meaning winter.

Hiemal-class items are then like hibernating animals I think. They're in a state of dormancy and basically trying to contain it just makes the problem worse.

Like removing or messing with a keystone species.

The two examples I read had the group of people who ate one another and that messing with them led to some sort of weird stuff with the trees or how dealing with DC Chaac was messing with the weather patterns.

In a sense, these anomalies that supposedly don't belong are actually vital components to a system.

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
If we pretend "Object Class" is and always has been "Containment Difficulty" (because that's what it is, really), then Hiemal doesn't fit into it.

Safe means "Really easy to contain"
Keter means "Really hard to contain"
Hiemal means "These two things contain either other to some extent" but then doesn't give us any information on how much extra effort the Foundation has to put into containing one/both of them.

I could see Safe-Hiemal and Keter-Hiemal etc being more useful in-universe, but that might just be too much information for Object Class

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
I'm surprised that nobody asked the most obvious question that could be asked: Why is this object class named "Hiemal"? Every other object class name has some degree of meaningfulness to it:

  • Safe & Neutralized: self-explanatory.
  • Euclid: obvious allusion to the real-life Greek mathematician, who deduced the principles of Euclidean geometry and thus is indirectly responsible for our modern understanding of non-Euclidean geometry (AKA "batshit-weird geometry where it's possible to have an infinitely long line intersect only one of two parallel lines", which is the the kind of weirdness you'd expect from Euclid-class anomalies).
  • Keter: Named after the topmost sephira in the Tree of Life, and literally means "crown", alluding to how objects of this class are of top priority for containment due to being extremely hazardous to normalcy if not human/universal existence.
  • Thaumiel: The shadow of Keter, as the topmost of the Qliphoth.
  • Embla: Name of the first woman in Norse mythology. Is used for an SCP-001 that is about the source of all anomalies in existence.
  • Apollyon: Greek name of Abaddon, either a place of destruction/death/realm of the dead or an angel of similarly dire attributes. Literally means "destroyer".
  • Maksur: Arabic for "broken". So far it's only applied to a Broken God-related skip article where the anomaly in question was a flawed attempt at recreating the "Broken God" that was eventually destroyed — in effect, a "broken" miniature of the "Broken God" that was broken by the GOC into its component pieces that have since then remained inert, yet the anomaly itself is not considered "Neutralized" due to a likelihood of them spontaneously reactivating.

Compared to all of these, "Hiemal" stands out for its meaning ("wintry") not having any obvious relevance to its usage (whether it's "the anomaly you contained was acting as a box for another anomaly" or "a system of two anomalies that both require containment, but which also actively serve as containment for each other").

item.title: Idea:
item.content:encoded:
I would use it. Why? Because it is an organization, and at times, long running and far reaching organizations have a disconnect with modern and tradition. In universe, this debate would be happening! This thread is the perfect example of how the Foundation would look:

Scientist A: I think we need a new class.
Scientist B: nah nah nah, we have enough already, we don't need a redundant one.
Scientist C: Well, it might not be as redundant, they still have differences.
Scientist A: SEE!
Scientist B: It still is not different enough to warrant a new class, and think of the previous finds that share those traits but don't have a special class
Scientist A: They are different enough, and we could change them to meet the standard.
Scientist B: That would take time, resources and overall be a pain

You get the idea.

So you could make the article with that designation, but you could also add a note by someone saying that the class is unnecessary. For further authenticity, you could have someone else EDIT it so it actually feels like a document edited by a peer….because it is….
Now, I do not mean to say that we should all start making our own designations, but I do think that toying with the idea now and then would provide a glimpse of the Foundation's inner workings.

Maybe a couple people could use it before it "dies off" in and out of universe.

Edit: I forgot the > had to have a space after it to work…without the space it just removes the text….I got an idea for a format screw….

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
I'm in the same field as Bleep. I don't expect Hiemal to become a normal object class. It's definition is too narrow to do that.

That said, I think it falls into the same category as Apollyon and Maksur. In that it's an object class that serves as a narrative tool instead of being a requirement for an article. I do want to see more Heimals and Apollyons, as they're often very interesting articles. We are a creative writing community that uses an experimental format already, so I think using Heimal works just fine if someone wants to push that format a little bit further.

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
Gonna weigh in here and say, that although I think 3700 exemplifies the exact definition of what Niles was going for (IE a naturally balanced system of interactions between two anomalies, wherein each entity's effects counterbalances and neutralizes the others, and when the Foundation intervenes, and destabilizes this balance, it causes serious issues) I do not feel as if this can become a prevalent or standard class. Others in this thread have echoed sentiments of why this is, but I'm going to be honest. The class is far too specific, it denotes a very unique and narrow relationship between an two anomalies that exists in maybe 3 or 4 articles on the wiki.

The primary reason I used it in 3700, and not Thaumiel/Keter is due to feedback I'd received from parties insisting that it wasn't Thaumiel, due to the disruption of normalcy that 3700-1 causes, and it doesn't quite fit in Keter because of the way 3700-1 and 3700-2 mitigate each other. Hiemal represents the intersection of those 2 classes, in a very very narrow range, and thus isn't really a vehicle for a distinctive new class in which to place SCPs, and I don't wish to see it become something that's used regularly because of this.

I still don't see how Thaumiel wouldn't apply.

Thaumiel-class objects are highly classified and extremely rare anomalies that are utilized by the Foundation to contain or counteract the effects of other highly dangerous anomalies, especially Keter-class objects.

What you're proposing seems to be nothing more than a glorified version of SCP-2932 or Roget's Proposal. If one anomaly is containing the other, then both together could be considered as Thaumiel - or, at worst, Keter-Thaumiel. "Hiemal" doesn't do anything that Thaumiel doesn't already.

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
I'd like to amend the definition of Hiemal, actually, as it's going to be more effective as used in this way: it's in essence a system of two or more distinct but related anomalies that keep each other in check.

3240 is this, as is 3700. These are distinct from Thaumiel as they in essence serve as their OWN containment - they can't be applied to other SCPs to contain them, and attempts to contain one with traditional methods will result in issues with the other participants. There may be a need for concealment, as with 3700, or disinformation campaigns to hide their existence from the public, but they should not have a net anomalous effect.

2339 would not be Hiemal, as the two creatures involved weren't found together and weren't related. The objects in Roget's proposal, however, would be.

item.title: Re: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
Hmm… I feel like you've successfully produced a rich, complex narrative, and now you're trying to put a label on that. You've got a story about the Foundation pulling one string and discovering that the world is a rich tapestry beyond their previous scope, which they've potentially seriously fucked up. That's cool. I can think of maybe a couple existing articles like that.

But, in terms of impact:
- Would having this word actually encourage people to write more stories like this?
- What narrative purpose can letting your readers know at the outset "Herein resides the story of the Foundation's hubris and what the containment of an anomaly did show them" serve?

I doubt the first, and I really don't see how revealing that to the reader is going to add anything. Euclid and Keter build expectations that something is going to be weird or dangerous, respectively. Heimal just sounds like "this is going to be a narratively complex one" or maybe presaging the entire specific story frame you mention, to the reader, up front. Why?

item.title: Hiemal Class Discussion
item.content:encoded:
So, after posting my 3k proposal as a mainlist SCP, I changed the object class from Keter to Hiemal.

In terms of the locked box test, I'd describe it as such: "You contained the box for something else. Oops."

In essence, this class would be used for anomalies which, themselves, combat or suppress the effects of another anomaly. Containing or neutralizing the Hiemal class object results in that other anomaly surfacing.

It wouldn't be common, but it could be used to put the Foundation in interesting dilemmas, and force them to come to interesting solutions.

But yeah. Anyone think of any other articles on the site that might fit this tag? Can you see this becoming an accepted class?
